# [Make.com for Small Business: Is It Worth Using in 2026?](https://inclusiveaihub.org/2026/10/01/make-com-for-small-business-is-it-worth-using-in-2026/)

![](https://i0.wp.com/inclusiveaihub.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/inclusiveaihub-Make.com-for-Small-Business-Is-It-Worth-Using-in-2026-1.png?resize=1400%2C933&ssl=1 "Make.com for Small Business: Is It Worth Using in 2026?")

_An independent, evidence-led review from InclusiveAIHub — looking past the marketing to the features, pricing, and governance questions that actually matter for small teams._

If you’ve typed “**is Make.com worth it for small business**” into a search bar, you’re probably staring down a familiar small-business problem: too many manual tasks, too few hands, and a dozen apps that don’t talk to each other. Make.com (formerly Integromat) is one of the most recommended answers to that problem — but “most recommended” and “right for _your_ business” aren’t always the same thing.

At InclusiveAIHub, we don’t just look at what a platform _does_ — we look at how it handles your data while doing it. This review combines a practical small-business lens with the governance scrutiny we apply to every platform in our [AI Compliance Directory](https://inclusiveaihub.org/ai-compliance-directory/).

**Quick take:** Make.com is a strong fit for small businesses that want visual, no-code automation with room to grow into AI-powered workflows — provided you pick the right plan and understand how your data is handled. You can [start on Make.com’s free plan here](https://www.make.com/en/register?pc=inclusiveaihub) to test the waters before committing to anything.

* * *

## What Is Make.com?

Make.com is a visual, no-code automation and integration platform that lets you connect different apps and services into automated workflows — called **scenarios** — without writing a line of code. Think: “When a new lead fills out my website form, add them to my CRM, send a Slack notification, and email them a welcome sequence” — built by dragging and connecting modules on a canvas rather than coding an API integration yourself.

Originally launched as Integromat, the platform was acquired by Celonis (an enterprise process-intelligence company) in 2020 and rebranded to Make in 2022. It now connects 3,000+ applications and is used by hundreds of thousands of businesses worldwide, from solo founders to enterprise operations teams.

For small businesses specifically, Make.com’s appeal is simple: it replaces hours of repetitive admin work — data entry, follow-up emails, spreadsheet updates, cross-app syncing — with automation you can build yourself, without hiring a developer.

* * *

## Key Features That Matter for Small Business

### 1\. Visual, No-Code Scenario Builder

You build automations on a drag-and-drop canvas, which makes it genuinely usable for non-technical founders and operations staff — not just developers. You can see every step of a workflow, which also makes troubleshooting far easier than with a black-box automation tool.

### 2\. 3,000+ App Integrations

From Google Workspace and Shopify to Stripe, HubSpot, QuickBooks, and social platforms, Make.com’s integration library covers most of the tools a small business already runs on. If an app isn’t natively supported, Make also supports custom API connections and webhooks.

### 3\. Maia — A Conversational AI Co-Worker

This is where Make.com has pulled ahead of a lot of small-business automation tools recently. **Maia by Make** lets you describe what you want in plain language — e.g., _“When a new lead is added to my CRM, send a summary to Slack”_ — and it builds the automation for you inside the visual builder, step by step, so you can review it before anything runs. For a small business without an in-house “automation person,” this materially lowers the learning curve.

### 4\. Make AI Agents

Beyond simple triggers-and-actions, Make AI Agents let workflows make context-aware decisions in real time — useful for things like routing customer inquiries, qualifying leads, or triaging support tickets without hard-coding every possible rule. You can choose which underlying AI model powers an agent, which matters for cost and data-handling reasons (more on that below).

### 5\. Operations-Based Pricing (Not Per-User, at Entry Level)

Unlike some competitors that charge per user from day one, Make’s entry-level plans are priced around monthly “operations” (actions performed), which tends to suit small teams with lighter, shared usage better than strict per-seat pricing.

* * *

## Make.com Pricing for Small Business (2026)

Make.com uses a free-forever tier plus four paid tiers, priced by monthly operations rather than purely by seat count at the lower tiers. Pricing below reflects typical published rates as of 2026 — always confirm current pricing on [Make.com’s official pricing page](https://www.make.com/en/register?pc=inclusiveaihub), since automation vendors adjust tiers periodically.

| Plan | Approx. Price | Monthly Operations | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Free** | $0  | 1,000 | Testing the platform, very light automation |
| **Core** | ~$9/mo (annual) | 10,000 | Small businesses automating their first real workflows |
| **Pro** | ~$16/mo (annual) | 10,000 + priority execution | Small teams needing faster, more reliable execution |
| **Teams** | ~$29/mo (annual) | 10,000 + collaboration features | Small businesses with multiple people building/managing automations |
| **Enterprise** | Custom quote | Custom | Businesses needing isolated infrastructure, SSO, and extended SLAs |

**Small-business takeaway:** Most solo founders and small teams start comfortably on **Core**, and move to **Pro** once execution speed and log visibility start to matter. The free plan is genuinely useful for proving out your first automation before you pay anything — [you can create a free account here](https://www.make.com/en/register?pc=inclusiveaihub) and estimate your real operation volume before choosing a paid tier.

One thing to watch: operations add up faster than workflow count suggests — each individual action inside a scenario (a read, a write, an update) typically counts as one operation. If you’re automating high-volume processes (e.g., syncing hundreds of orders a day), model your expected usage against the credit limits before committing to an annual plan.

* * *
